Roll of Thunder, Hear My Cry, Mildred D. Taylor's novel that won the Newbery Medal in 1977. The book tells the story of the Logan family, a resilient Black household in nineteen-thirty Mississippi, navigating racial segregation, economic hardship, and the constant struggle to maintain dignity and family integrity. We see this world through the eyes of Cassie Logan, a spirited nine-year-old who becomes increasingly aware of the injustices and humiliations of segregation as the novel progresses, especially after a harrowing encounter with white racism in a store. Her parents, Mary and David Logan, own their land—rare and precious for a Black family—and they struggle constantly to keep it while resisting both economic exploitation and social pressure to submit to racial hierarchy. The novel includes a subplot about the family's moral response when a white man dies in confrontation with one of their neighbors. The Logans refuse to participate in or condone the violence, but they also refuse to betray their community. What Taylor does that was revolutionary for children's literature is to use the interior perspective of a Black child to center Black agency, humanity, and familial love rather than positioning Black characters as victims observed from outside. The novel explores the price of self-respect, the bonds of family and community, and the ways that love sustains resistance to dehumanization. In doing so, it transformed the landscape of young-adult fiction by centering a Black girl's emotional and moral life.
